concepts.name: Logarithms and iterated logarithm notation
concepts.gloss: The base-2 logarithm lg n = ceil(log2 n), its rules (log of a product, change of base), and the meaning of powers such as (lg n)^(1-kappa).

concepts.name: Big-Omega, Theta and little-o notation
concepts.gloss: Asymptotic lower bounds Omega, tight bounds Theta and strictly smaller order o, used alongside O to compare running times.

concepts.name: Binary representation and bit operations
concepts.gloss: Writing non-negative integers (and signed ones in two's complement) as bit strings, and the bitwise operations XOR, AND and shifts, including the number of ones in a bit string.

concepts.name: Modular arithmetic
concepts.gloss: Arithmetic on integers modulo m, congruence classes, and the cyclic group Z/m under addition.

concepts.name: Primes, coprimality and gcd
concepts.gloss: Prime numbers, greatest common divisors, pairwise coprime integers, and the fact that primes of a given size are plentiful and can be found by search.

concepts.name: Chinese remainder theorem
concepts.gloss: For pairwise coprime moduli, the map from Z/(m1...mk) to the product of Z/mi given by reduction is a bijection (ring isomorphism).

concepts.name: Roots of unity
concepts.gloss: The complex solutions of z^n = 1, namely e^{2πik/n}, with Euler's formula e^{iθ} = cos θ + i sin θ and the fact that their powers sum to zero in the nontrivial case.

concepts.name: Vectors, matrices and invertibility
concepts.gloss: Vectors, linear maps and matrices over R, C or F2, matrix products and inverses, triangular and permutation matrices, and linear combinations.

concepts.name: Finite field F2 arithmetic
concepts.gloss: The field with elements 0 and 1 in which addition is XOR and multiplication is AND, over which vector spaces of bit vectors are studied.

concepts.name: Permutations and Cartesian products
concepts.gloss: Bijections of finite sets, product index sets [a1]x...x[at], and listing multi-indexed arrays in lexicographic (row-major) order.

concepts.name: Floor, ceiling and summation notation
concepts.gloss: Rounding down and up, finite and geometric sums, and indicator notation.

concepts.name: Recurrences and induction
concepts.gloss: Defining a cost by a recurrence, bounding it by induction or unrolling, and the divide-and-conquer pattern T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n).

concepts.name: Norms, absolute values and error bounds
concepts.gloss: The modulus of a complex number, the maximum norm of a vector, the triangle inequality, and how to bound accumulated rounding errors and then round to the nearest integer.

concepts.name: Fast Fourier transform and divide and conquer
concepts.gloss: The standard O(n log n) evaluation of a length-2^k DFT by splitting into halves, and its use to multiply polynomials via pointwise products.

concepts.name: Sorting and data movement on tapes
concepts.gloss: Ordinary sorting and merging of lists, and the idea that a tape machine reads and writes sequentially, so rearranging data costs scans rather than random access.

concepts.name: Finite alphabet encodings and constant-factor simulation
concepts.gloss: Storing data in a fixed finite alphabet, packing a constant number of symbols per cell, and simulating one machine by another with a constant-factor time change.

concepts.name: Ring and group notions for polynomials
concepts.gloss: Sets with addition and multiplication satisfying the usual laws, polynomial reduction modulo a fixed polynomial, and maps preserving both operations.

common-frame-principle.name: scalar ring
common-frame-principle.meaning: The ring the network's scalars and gate coefficients lie in, F_2 for the bit network and Z[i,1/2] for the complex one.
common-frame-principle.quote: Replace each scalar of the [linear exchange network](linear-network.md) by an array in $R^\Omega$, where $R$ is the scalar ring and $\Omega$ a finite address set shared by all wires, and apply each gate at every address; call the result $\mathsf S_\Omega$.

common-frame-principle.name: address set
common-frame-principle.meaning: The finite set of addresses, shared by all wires, that indexes the entries of each wire's array.
common-frame-principle.quote: Replace each scalar of the [linear exchange network](linear-network.md) by an array in $R^\Omega$, where $R$ is the scalar ring and $\Omega$ a finite address set shared by all wires, and apply each gate at every address; call the result $\mathsf S_\Omega$.

common-frame-principle.name: array network
common-frame-principle.meaning: The network obtained by applying each scalar gate at every address, acting on the vector of all wire arrays.
common-frame-principle.quote: Replace each scalar of the [linear exchange network](linear-network.md) by an array in $R^\Omega$, where $R$ is the scalar ring and $\Omega$ a finite address set shared by all wires, and apply each gate at every address; call the result $\mathsf S_\Omega$.

common-frame-principle.name: vertex
common-frame-principle.meaning: A vertex of a wire: its source, a gate on it, or its sink.
common-frame-principle.quote: At each vertex $v$ (source, gate or sink) choose an invertible $R$-linear frame $D_v$ on $R^\Omega$; unlike a gate, it may mix addresses.

common-frame-principle.name: frame
common-frame-principle.meaning: The invertible R-linear operator on R^Omega chosen at vertex v, so that the stored array there is D_v applied to the logical array.
common-frame-principle.quote: At each vertex $v$ (source, gate or sink) choose an invertible $R$-linear frame $D_v$ on $R^\Omega$; unlike a gate, it may mix addresses.

common-frame-principle.name: edge start vertex
common-frame-principle.meaning: The vertex at the start of an edge whose end is v.
common-frame-principle.quote: All wires at a gate share its frame; an edge from $u$ to $v$ applies the change of frame $D_vD_u^{-1}$.

common-frame-principle.name: role
common-frame-principle.meaning: A role, the fixed name of a wire in the network.
common-frame-principle.quote: $D_{\rm in}$ applies $D_{\mathrm{source}(w)}$ to the input array on each role $w$; $D_{\rm out}$ applies $D_{\mathrm{sink}(w)}$ to each output.

common-frame-principle.name: input frame operator
common-frame-principle.meaning: The operator applying the source frame of each input role to that role's array.
common-frame-principle.quote: $D_{\rm in}$ applies $D_{\mathrm{source}(w)}$ to the input array on each role $w$; $D_{\rm out}$ applies $D_{\mathrm{sink}(w)}$ to each output.

common-frame-principle.name: output frame operator
common-frame-principle.meaning: The operator applying the sink frame of each output role to that role's array.
common-frame-principle.quote: $D_{\rm in}$ applies $D_{\mathrm{source}(w)}$ to the input array on each role $w$; $D_{\rm out}$ applies $D_{\mathrm{sink}(w)}$ to each output.

common-frame-principle.name: physical input
common-frame-principle.meaning: The vector of input arrays actually supplied to the machine.
common-frame-principle.quote: Read a physical input $f$ as the logical input $g=D_{\rm in}^{-1}f$; no work is done.

common-frame-principle.name: logical input
common-frame-principle.meaning: The logical input D_in^{-1} f, the arrays the stored input represents.
common-frame-principle.quote: Read a physical input $f$ as the logical input $g=D_{\rm in}^{-1}f$; no work is done.

common-frame-principle.name: edge logical array
common-frame-principle.meaning: The logical array carried by a wire along one edge.
common-frame-principle.quote: An edge carrying logical array $\varphi$ turns stored $D_u\varphi$ into $D_v\varphi$.

common-frame-principle.name: gate logical input
common-frame-principle.meaning: The logical array on the j-th wire entering a gate.
common-frame-principle.quote: A gate outputs combinations $\sum_jc_j\varphi_j$ of its logical inputs $\varphi_j$, with coefficients $c_j\in R$ equal at every address, so by linearity $\sum_jc_jD_v\varphi_j=D_v\sum_jc_j\varphi_j$: the shared frame commutes with the gate.

common-frame-principle.name: gate coefficient
common-frame-principle.meaning: The coefficient in R with which a gate output combines its j-th input, the same at every address.
common-frame-principle.quote: A gate outputs combinations $\sum_jc_j\varphi_j$ of its logical inputs $\varphi_j$, with coefficients $c_j\in R$ equal at every address, so by linearity $\sum_jc_jD_v\varphi_j=D_v\sum_jc_j\varphi_j$: the shared frame commutes with the gate.

common-frame-principle.name: role permutation
common-frame-principle.meaning: The permutation of roles sending each input role to its output role, swapping the two banks and fixing scratch roles.
common-frame-principle.quote: The exchange network sends input role $w$ to output role $\rho(w)$ with sign $\varepsilon_w=\pm1$, where $\rho$ swaps the two banks and fixes every scratch role.

common-frame-principle.name: route sign
common-frame-principle.meaning: The sign, plus or minus one, that the exchange network attaches to the value on input role w.
common-frame-principle.quote: The exchange network sends input role $w$ to output role $\rho(w)$ with sign $\varepsilon_w=\pm1$, where $\rho$ swaps the two banks and fixes every scratch role.

common-frame-principle.name: role logical array
common-frame-principle.meaning: The part of the logical input g on input role w.
common-frame-principle.quote: So $\mathsf S_\Omega$ moves the logical array $g_w$ of $w$ to role $\rho(w)$ as $\varepsilon_wg_w$, and the route from $w$ applies $\varepsilon_wD_{\mathrm{sink}(\rho(w))}D_{\mathrm{source}(w)}^{-1}$ to its input array, scratch roles included.

common-frame-principle.name: consecutive wire vertices
common-frame-principle.meaning: Three consecutive vertices along one wire.
common-frame-principle.quote: Interior frames cancel because edge changes telescope, $(D_{v_2}D_{v_1}^{-1})(D_{v_1}D_{v_0}^{-1})=D_{v_2}D_{v_0}^{-1}$ for consecutive vertices $v_0,v_1,v_2$ on a wire, and gates let their frame through; they only set edge costs.

common-frame-principle.name: first address chunk
common-frame-principle.meaning: The address chunk of m fields that the bit-procedure frames shift.
common-frame-principle.quote: In the bit procedure, addresses contain two chunks $h,d$ of $m$ fields each; vertex $v$ gets a rational $m\times m$ matrix $M_v$ and the frame $\Phi_{M_v}$ moving the entry at $(h,d)$ to $(h+M_vd,\,d)$.

common-frame-principle.name: second address chunk
common-frame-principle.meaning: The address chunk of m fields by which the bit-procedure frames shift h.
common-frame-principle.quote: In the bit procedure, addresses contain two chunks $h,d$ of $m$ fields each; vertex $v$ gets a rational $m\times m$ matrix $M_v$ and the frame $\Phi_{M_v}$ moving the entry at $(h,d)$ to $(h+M_vd,\,d)$.

common-frame-principle.name: fields per chunk
common-frame-principle.meaning: The number of address fields in each of the chunks h and d.
common-frame-principle.quote: In the bit procedure, addresses contain two chunks $h,d$ of $m$ fields each; vertex $v$ gets a rational $m\times m$ matrix $M_v$ and the frame $\Phi_{M_v}$ moving the entry at $(h,d)$ to $(h+M_vd,\,d)$.

common-frame-principle.name: frame matrix
common-frame-principle.meaning: The fixed rational m by m matrix attached to vertex v in the bit procedure.

common-frame-principle.name: shear frame
common-frame-principle.meaning: The frame moving the array entry at (h,d) to (h + M_v d, d).

common-frame-principle.quote: Replace each scalar of the [linear exchange network](linear-network.md) by an array in $R^\Omega$, where $R$ is the scalar ring and $\Omega$ a finite address set shared by all wires, and apply each gate at every address; call the result $\mathsf S_\Omega$.
The cost of an edge is counted by the [rank](linear-algebra-basics.md) of $M_v-M_u$, one smaller interchange per unit

background.summary: The reader has an undergraduate computer science education: discrete mathematics (modular arithmetic, primes and coprimality, the Chinese remainder theorem, permutations, induction, recurrences), calculus-level analysis (logarithms, floor and ceiling, norms and rounding errors), linear algebra (vectors, matrices, invertibility, rank, over the reals, complex numbers and F2), and algorithms (asymptotic notation, schoolbook multiplication, divide and conquer, sorting) with a first look at the FFT. They know basic multitape Turing machines and tapes, polynomials and complex numbers including roots of unity. They have not met Schoenhage-Strassen or Karatsuba-level multiplication algorithms in depth, ring and group-algebra language beyond polynomials, tensor products, numerical error analysis of fixed-point transforms, or any research literature on integer multiplication.
